title: Digital & Product Strategy
metaTitle: Digital & Product Strategy Consulting · Artifact Digital
description: Digital and product strategy that finds where purpose-built software can create real business leverage — then decides what to build first, what to defer, and why.
lede: Strategy is how we identify where purpose-built software can create meaningful business leverage — the workflow, the knowledge, the customer experience or the product opportunity worth building for — and turn it into choices a team can act on.
summary: Where purpose-built software creates business leverage, and what to build first.
intro: Digital strategy is one of the most abused phrases in our industry. It gets used to describe everything from a marketing campaign to a technology roadmap to a vague sense that a company should "do more online." So let's be precise about what we mean.

Strategy is a set of choices about where you'll compete and how you'll win — and, just as importantly, what you won't do. For us, those choices lead somewhere concrete: the software and experiences your customers, employees and partners actually use. Strategy is the connective tissue between a business goal and the thing someone taps.

When strategy is missing, you can feel it. Teams argue about features instead of outcomes. Every stakeholder gets their box on the homepage. The roadmap is a list of everyone's wishes, ranked by who complained loudest. The work is rarely to invent something new — it's to make the hard choices the organization has been avoiding.

sections.heading: We start with the business, not the interface
body: It's tempting to open a strategy engagement by auditing the website or the product. We don't start there. We start with the P&L, the growth targets, and the friction the leadership team feels but hasn't named yet. If we don't understand how the business makes money and where it's trying to go, any recommendation we make about design or technology is just taste.

So the first conversations are about outcomes. What has to be true in eighteen months? Where is revenue leaking? Where is expertise trapped in spreadsheets and inboxes? Which customer segments matter most, and which ones are quietly subsidizing the rest? Only once we understand the shape of the business do we look at software — and then the opportunities tend to announce themselves.

sections.heading: From brand to direction
body: Most companies already have a brand — a reputation, a voice, a way customers think about them. The job isn't to reinvent that. It's to carry it into the software and experiences you build next, so they feel unmistakably like you and clearly better than the alternative.

Our history in brand and agency work matters here. We translate that equity into concrete direction: how the product is positioned, the story it tells, the priorities it holds, and the experience it delivers. That direction becomes the brief every design and engineering decision is measured against.

sections.heading: The experience is the strategy
body: For most modern companies, the experience is the strategy. Your customers don't experience your org chart or your tech stack. They experience the thing in front of them — how quickly they found what they needed, whether it felt trustworthy, whether it respected their time. That experience is where strategy either becomes real or falls apart.

This is why we refuse to separate strategy from design and build into tidy phases handed between different teams. A strategy that can't be designed is a fantasy. A design that ignores the business is decoration. We keep them in the same room, held by the same senior people, because that's where good decisions actually get made.

sections.heading: Prioritization is the whole game
body: Almost every organization we work with has more ideas than capacity. The value of a strategy isn't the ideas — it's the sequence. What do you do first, what do you deliberately defer, and what do you kill? A good roadmap makes tradeoffs visible so leadership can make them on purpose instead of by accident.

We're opinionated here. We'll tell you when a beloved initiative isn't worth the effort — including when the right answer is off-the-shelf software rather than something custom — and we'll show our reasoning. You don't need a partner who agrees with you. You need one who's spent enough time in the arena to know which battles are worth fighting.

inMethod.body: We find where software can create real leverage — the workflow that costs the most, the knowledge nobody's tools use, the product no one has built yet — and what has to be true for it to pay off.
Strategy gets tested as working software, not defended in a deck. Early prototypes show whether the opportunity holds up before a major budget is committed.
We tie what the software should achieve to measures leadership already cares about, and read real usage against them.
The roadmap stays a set of deliberate choices — what's next, what waits, what stops — as the business and the software change.

deliverables: A clear view of where software can create leverage, and what it must achieve for the business
A current-state assessment that names where value is leaking and why
Positioning and direction for the product or experience you're building next
A prioritized, sequenced roadmap with the rationale for every tradeoff
Success measures that connect the software to business results
A first, concrete move — often a prototype, not a plan to make a plan
whoFor: Leadership teams who feel the friction but can't agree on what to build first
Companies weighing whether a new platform or product is worth building at all
Organizations whose digital footprint has sprawled beyond anyone's control
Brands with strong equity that hasn't yet been carried into their software

faq.q: How is this different from a marketing or SEO strategy?
faq.a: Marketing strategy is about how you reach and persuade an audience. Digital and product strategy is about what an organization builds and delivers — the software and experiences people actually use — and how that serves the business. Marketing and SEO are inputs to it, not substitutes for it.

faq.q: Do we need to have our goals figured out before we start?
faq.a: No. Half the value of the work is helping leadership get honest and specific about goals. Most teams have goals — they just haven't reconciled the competing ones or made the tradeoffs explicit. That reconciliation is part of the work.

faq.q: How long does strategy work take?
faq.a: Long enough to make the hard decisions, and no longer. Scope depends on the size of the organization and how much research already exists, and we'll propose a timeline once we understand it. Strategy work that drags on for months usually means the hard decisions are being avoided.

faq.q: What happens after the strategy is delivered?
faq.a: It keeps going. Because the same senior team carries it into research, design and engineering, there's no handoff cliff — the strategy usually becomes the first prototype. We can also support your internal teams, or hand off a plan clear enough that someone else can run it.
